# Block 4: Context, disclosure and autonomy {.unnumbered} Two questions decide how far you can trust anything an AI assistant does with your code: 1. **What can it see?** Its answers are only as good as its context, and everything it sees has left your machine. 2. **What can it do?** An assistant that advises leaves you as the filter on every change. An agent that acts removes that filter. This block covers both, using Claude Code in the terminal. If you use Posit Assistant instead, the collapsed boxes give the differences. *⏱ ~33 minutes* # Part A: What can the assistant see? {.unnumbered} | Surface | Example | What it can see | Can it act? | |---|---|---|---| | Browser chat | Any chat website | What you paste | No | | Terminal agent | Claude Code | Project files, and the output of any command it runs | Yes, in your files and shell | | Session-aware IDE assistant | Posit Assistant in RStudio or Positron | Your live R session (loaded packages, data frames, console history) and project files | Yes, in your session and files | :::{.callout-note} **Knowing versus guessing.** An assistant can describe your data confidently for two quite different reasons: it has been given real information, or it is recalling patterns from training data. Only the first is reliable. It has real information when you pasted the output, when it read a file, when the IDE injected your session, or when it ran code and read the result. It is guessing when none of those apply. The tells are a well-known dataset you never mentioned (`mtcars`, `iris`, `penguins`) or column names and values you never supplied. Even with context, a model's account of *what it can see* is unreliable. Check any data-specific claim against the real object. ::: ## Exercise 1: Context decides the answer :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} The same error, three levels of context (10 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **1. Error only.** In a browser chat, open a fresh session and paste only this, asking "What does this error mean?": ``` Error in `mutate()`: ℹ In argument: `mass_change = mass_post - mass_pre_g`. Caused by error: ! object 'mass_post' not found ``` The answer can only reason from the error text. **2. Error plus code plus structure.** In a new session, paste: ``` I am running this code: voles |> mutate(mass_change = mass_post - mass_pre_g) and getting: Error in `mutate()`: ℹ In argument: `mass_change = mass_post - mass_pre_g`. Caused by error: ! object 'mass_post' not found The data structure is: Rows: 72 Columns: 6 $ subject_id "V001", "V002", "V003", ... $ sex "M", "F", "M", ... $ treatment_arm "Control", "Control", ... $ mass_pre_g 28.3, 27.9, 30.1, ... $ mass_post_g 28.5, 28.0, 30.5, ... $ metabolic_rate_post 13.21, 12.84, 13.55, ... What is wrong? ``` It should name the missing `_g` suffix. **3. No paste at all.** Save the failing code in a script in your project. Start Claude Code from the project folder and ask only: "Why does the mutate() call in my script fail?" Claude Code can open the script and run code to inspect the data. Then ask: "How do you know the column names?" Compare its answer with what you know it was given. If it claims to have seen something it could not have seen, you have found the unreliability described in the callout above. :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Using Posit Assistant Load the data in your R session and run the failing code, then ask Posit Assistant only: "Why did my last command fail?" A session-aware assistant can read your console history and the data frame without your pasting anything. ::: :::: ::: The lesson is not that one route is correct. The answer is only as good as the context, and context reaches the model by more than one route. ## Disclosure: every route out of your machine Everything an assistant sees is sent to a model provider. Data leave your machine by four routes: 1. **What you paste.** Errors, outputs, printed results. 2. **Files it reads.** A data file in the repository or project folder. 3. **Session context the IDE injects.** Posit Assistant reads loaded packages, data frames and console history, so a data frame in memory can reach the model without any paste. 4. **Output of commands it runs.** If an agent runs `print(voles)` or `head data.csv`, those values enter its context. Before you decide what to show, know what the surface can already reach. A data file committed to the repository, or a tibble loaded in your session, may already be disclosed. When you describe a data frame deliberately, three commands reveal increasing amounts: - `names(voles)` lists column names only, in their original order. - `summary(voles)` adds ranges, quartiles and missing-value counts for numeric columns: the shape of the data, not individual records. - `glimpse(voles)` or `str(voles)` adds the first few actual values of every column. :::{.callout-important} **Before using an assistant on research data**, check three things: whether your institution permits sending this kind of data to this provider; whether your ethics approval and data-sharing agreements allow it; and whether a synthetic or anonymised copy would serve instead. Tool settings that restrict reading (see the [enforced-controls block](11f-enforced-controls.qmd)) reduce accidental exposure, but they do not make an agent safe for confidential data: any command it runs that prints data sends that data to the provider. For personal or confidential data, let the agent work on a synthetic copy and run the final code on the real data yourself, outside the agent's workspace. Hooks and project settings are also code that runs on your machine, and a cloned repository can carry its own; trust only repositories whose configuration you have read. ::: ## Context you hold in your head *Instructor demonstration, about 3 minutes.* A data file can supply column names and types, but not your scientific question or your design intent. Your instructor will ask a fresh chat this: ``` I have a dataset with pre and post measurements. How should I analyse it? ``` and then, in a new session, this: ``` I have 72 voles, balanced across three treatment arms (Control, Low_dose, High_dose) and two sexes (M, F). Each animal has body mass measured before and after treatment, and a single post-treatment metabolic-rate reading. My question is whether the high-dose treatment changes mass relative to control, and whether the effect differs between sexes. The dataset is small (n = 12 per cell). I will report effect sizes alongside any inferential test. Given this design, what is a defensible primary analysis, and what are the main threats to its validity? ``` The first returns a tour of options (paired tests, change scores, ANCOVA, mixed models); the second can return a recommendation, because the design and the question now exist outside your head. Treat even the better answer as a proposal to check against a statistics text or a colleague. Choosing the primary analysis is your decision, not the assistant's. # Part B: What can the assistant do? {.unnumbered} The model is the same at every level below. What changes is what it is permitted to do, and therefore where you sit in the loop. | Rung | What happens | Claude Code | Posit Assistant | |---|---|---|---| | 0. Suggest | Completes the line you are typing | — | Next Edit Suggestions | | 1. Ask | Answers; changes nothing | Ask a question in `plan` mode | Ask mode | | 2. Plan | Proposes steps; changes nothing until you approve | `plan` mode | `/plan` | | 3. Act, with approval | Edits files and runs commands, asking first | `default` mode | Normal mode | | 4. Act, partly unsupervised | Some actions without asking | `acceptEdits` mode | Auto mode | | 5. Act, unsupervised | No prompts | `bypassPermissions` | YOLO mode | A sixth rung, acting remotely on a branch and returning a pull request, is covered in *Going further* below. In Claude Code, `Shift+Tab` cycles `default`, `acceptEdits` and `plan`. In Posit Assistant, `/plan`, `/auto`, `/yolo` and `/restricted` switch modes. Use rungs 0 to 3 throughout this course. Do not use rung 5. :::{.callout-warning} **Read the rung's small print.** `acceptEdits` in Claude Code approves more than edits: it also auto-approves common file commands such as `mkdir`, `touch`, `mv` and `cp`. A `cp` that overwrites a raw data file needs no approval in that mode. Posit Assistant's auto mode replaces your judgement with a classifier model's. Each step up the ladder removes a moment when you would have seen the action before it happened. **Approval fatigue is real.** At rung 3, an approval prompt you click through without reading is rung 5 with extra steps. The [enforced-controls block](11f-enforced-controls.qmd) covers the rules that hold however tired you are. ::: Higher rungs make standing instructions matter more. In Ask mode, a convention the assistant does not know costs you a re-read. In agent mode, the assistant acts on its guess, and the guess lands in your files. That is why the [instructions-and-skills block](11e-instructions-skills.qmd) comes next, and why the [enforced-controls block](11f-enforced-controls.qmd) follows it. ## Exercise 2: The same task, rising autonomy :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Ask, plan, act (15 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} Use your forked workshop repository, **committed and clean**, so every change is a diff you can inspect or revert. Never run an agent with uncommitted work you are not prepared to lose. **1. Ask.** Start Claude Code in plan mode (`claude --permission-mode plan`) and ask: ``` In scripts/clean_voles.R, how would I add a column mass_change equal to mass_post_g minus mass_pre_g? ``` Read the answer. Confirm with `git status` that nothing changed. **2. Plan.** Still in plan mode, give a goal that spans several files: ``` In the voles pipeline, add a derived mass_change column (mass_post_g minus mass_pre_g) in the cleaning step, create a new script that plots mass_change by treatment_arm, and make sure the pipeline still runs end to end. ``` Before approving, check that the plan names every file it will touch, does not touch raw data, says where the plot script goes, and says how it will check the pipeline runs. Amend the plan in conversation if any of that is missing. **3. Act, with approval.** Approve the plan and make sure you are in `default` mode, in which Claude Code asks before each edit or command (`Shift+Tab` switches modes). Read each approval prompt before answering it. Refuse at least one action you consider out of scope, and note how the agent responds. **4. Review.** When it finishes: ```bash git status git diff ``` Read the diff as you would a colleague's contribution. The agent's statement that the pipeline "still runs" is a claim; run the pipeline yourself to check it. **5. Compare.** At which rung did you decide the most? At which rung would you have missed an unwanted change if you had not read the diff? **6. Start your AI-use log.** Create `docs/ai-log.md` and write the first line yourself, rather than asking the agent, in the form set out in Block 1: ``` 2026-10-19; Claude Code (model as reported in the session); added mass_change and a plot script; kept both after reading the diff; rejected one out-of-scope edit. ``` Commit it with the agent's changes. You will add a line after each block in which an agent does work. :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Using Posit Assistant Use Ask mode for step 1, `/plan` for step 2, and Normal mode for step 3. The review in step 4 is the same: `git status` and `git diff` in the terminal. ::: :::: ::: :::{.callout-note} **Access and cost.** Plans and prices change; check before the session. - **Claude Code** needs an Anthropic account, used through a subscription or an API key; see Anthropic's documentation for current options. - **Posit Assistant** uses Posit AI Pass or your own provider key, including an Anthropic API key. In RStudio, providers are configured in the assistant's settings. - **GitHub Copilot** bills in AI credits; check GitHub's plans page for what your plan includes. - **Your institution** may have approved some of these tools and not others. ::: :::{.callout-note} ## Check · Reproduce · Record - **Check:** `git status` and `git diff` after every agent action; the agent's report that something "still runs" is a claim until you run it. - **Reproduce:** work only in a committed, clean repository, so every change is a diff you can inspect or revert. - **Record:** your AI-use log starts here, in `docs/ai-log.md`. ::: ## Check your understanding **You paste nothing, yet Claude Code names your columns correctly. How could it know them?**
**In Claude Code's acceptEdits mode, what does the agent do without asking?**
**Which check still works whatever rung the agent ran at?**
## Going further (not covered live) This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you. ### GitHub Copilot and the remote rung GitHub Copilot offers the same ladder in its own surfaces. Copilot Chat on github.com can also see files in the repository you open it from. | Rung | GitHub Copilot | |---|---| | 0. Suggest | Inline suggestions | | 1. Ask | Ask in Chat | | 2. Plan | Plan mode in the IDE | | 3. Act, with approval | Agent mode, approving each tool call | | 4. Act, partly unsupervised | Agent mode with auto-approval | | 5. Act, unsupervised | — | | 6. Act remotely | Cloud agent | The sixth rung, the **Copilot cloud agent**, works on the repository on GitHub, in an environment GitHub runs. It takes a task such as an issue, works on its own branch and returns a pull request. Copilot Free includes only limited agent features; check GitHub's plans page to see whether your plan includes the cloud agent. The cloud agent appears in the *Going further* section of the [characterisation-test block](11i-characterisation-tests.qmd), where its pull request meets a review gate. ### Exercise: context you hold in your head To try the demonstration above yourself, ask a fresh browser chat the first prompt, then a new session the second, and compare the answers. A data file can supply column names and types, but not your scientific question or your design intent. ## References - Claude Code documentation: *Permission modes*, . - Posit Assistant documentation: *Getting Started*, ; *Permissions & Trust*, . - GitHub documentation: *Plans for GitHub Copilot*, .
